draft.title: The bill of rights debate
card: A bill of rights is a document that lists the basic rights of people in a country. Australia has no national bill of rights.
say a bill of rights would protect rights better. It would set clear standards that governments must meet, and people could rely on them in court.
say it would hand power from parliament to unelected judges. They argue that elected members of parliament, who answer to voters, should decide how rights are balanced.
Victoria, the ACT and Queensland have their own human rights acts. These are state and territory laws and do not cover the whole country.
draft.remember: The debate is about who should protect rights: a bill of rights and the courts, or elected parliaments.

a.q: Which argument do opponents of a bill of rights make?
opts: It would shift power from parliament to unelected judges
It would give parliament too little power to make new laws
It would remove rights that people already have
It would apply to some states but not to the others
a.why: Opponents say judges, who are not elected, would gain power that now belongs to parliament. The option about removing rights is wrong because it is not the argument opponents make. Their concern is who decides, not the loss of rights.
a.clue: Think about who is elected and who is not.

b.q: Tariq says a national bill of rights would let a court strike down a rule made by elected members of parliament, and he opposes it for that reason. Which argument is he making?
opts: Judges would gain power that should stay with parliament
Rights would be less protected than they are now
Voters would have no way to enforce their rights
States would lose their own human rights acts
b.why: Tariq objects that unelected judges could override elected members of parliament. This is the opponents' argument about power moving from parliament to judges. Saying rights would be less protected is the tempting option, but it is a supporter-style concern about protection, which he does not raise.
b.clue: He is worried about who makes the final decision, not about how strong the rights are.

a.best: It would shift power from parliament to unelected judges

b.best: Judges would gain power that should stay with parliament

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about who is elected and who is not' points straight at the only option that mentions unelected judges, so a student can pick it without knowing the opponents' argument.

The why calls 'rights would be less protected' a supporter-style concern. Supporters argue a bill of rights would protect rights better, not less, so this label is confusing and misdescribes the supporters' side.
